Day 1
From Hotel: 4 min · 2 min → Tony Knowles Coastal Trail
1.Tony Knowles Coastal Trail
Alaska's most celebrated urban trail: 11 miles of paved path above Cook Inlet from Resolution Park to Kincaid Park. The views of the Alaska Range are extraordinary. In summer, beluga whales surface in the inlet and moose browse the vegetation beside the path.

7 min · 2 min → Anchorage Museum
2.Anchorage Museum
Alaska's largest museum, sharing the story of the state's art, history, science, and indigenous culture through world-class galleries. The Alaska Gallery traces 10,000 years of human life on this land — a proper primer for the rest of the trip.

3.Resolution Park
A compact waterfront deck centered on a bronze statue of Captain Cook, who anchored in Cook Inlet in 1778. On clear days Denali and the full Alaska Range rise above the skyline beyond the water — one of the finest urban panoramas in the state.

Day 2
From Hotel: 15 min → Alaska Native Heritage Center
1.Alaska Native Heritage Center
The world's premier center for Alaska Native cultures, with eleven indigenous groups represented through traditional dwellings, living demonstrations, and the Heritage Hall collection. Set on the shores of Lake Tiulana — an experience unlike any other museum on earth.

25 min → Flattop Mountain
2.Flattop Mountain
Alaska's most-climbed peak. A 1,350-foot ascent earns a 360° panorama: Anchorage below, Cook Inlet stretching west, and Denali visible to the north on clear days. The trail is straightforward but rocky near the summit — start early to beat summer crowds.

Day 3
From Hotel: 53 min → Alaska Wildlife Conservation Center
1.Alaska Wildlife Conservation Center
A 200-acre drive-through sanctuary 40 miles south of downtown. Grizzly bears, black bears, wood bison, moose, musk oxen, caribou, lynx, and wolves roam naturalistic enclosures. One of the finest accessible wildlife encounters in North America.

2.Portage Glacier
One of Alaska's most accessible glaciers, reached by a 1-hour cruise across iceberg-studded Portage Lake aboard the M/V Ptarmigan. Blue ice towers above the water at the glacier face. The Begich Boggs Visitor Center tells the stark story of the glacier's retreat since 1914.

3.Knik Glacier Helicopter Tour
A helicopter flight over the Chugach Range followed by a landing on Knik Glacier — a vast, slow-moving river of ice filling a mountain valley north of Palmer. The panoramas from the glacier surface are staggering: seracs, meltwater rivers, crevasse fields. The most viscerally Alaskan experience in this itinerary.

Day 4
From Hotel: 2h 12min → Matanuska Glacier
1.Matanuska Glacier
One of the largest road-accessible glaciers in the United States at 27 miles long. Guided walks lead onto the glacier surface past meltwater rivers, ice caves, and moraine fields. Crampons, helmets, and trekking poles provided. The scale only registers once you're standing on it.

66500 S Glacier Park Road · Sutton
2h 15min → Earthquake Park
2.Earthquake Park
On Good Friday 1964, a 9.2-magnitude earthquake — the largest ever recorded in North America — triggered a landslide that collapsed the Turnagain Heights neighborhood into Cook Inlet in minutes. The park preserves the fractured terrain: slumped bluffs, tilted earth, and Cook Inlet views reaching to the Alaska Range.

1.Exit Glacier
The only road-accessible section of Kenai Fjords National Park. A short walk leads to the glacier face, where dated stakes chart ice retreat across more than a century — one of the clearest physical records of climate change in the world. The Harding Icefield Trail climbs 3,000 feet above for vast icefield panoramas.

2.Kenai Fjords Wildlife Cruise
A 4-hour cruise from Seward's Small Boat Harbor into Resurrection Bay. Orcas, humpback whales, Steller sea lions, sea otters, tufted puffins, and bald eagles are regular sightings. Book the full-day cruise if staying overnight in Seward — it reaches tidewater glaciers in Kenai Fjords National Park itself.

Local Tastes
Smoked Salmon
Wild-caught Alaska salmon cured and smoked over alder wood. Intensely flavored and oil-rich — worlds apart from farmed fish. Available vacuum-sealed at specialty shops or as an entrée at dinner restaurants.
Alaska Sausage & Seafood· 10th & M Seafoods
Reindeer Sausage
Made from domesticated caribou raised by Alaska Native herders, blended with pork. Leaner than pork sausage with a mild gamey warmth. The classic: a bun with grilled onions and spicy mustard from 4th Avenue street carts.
4th Avenue street carts· Snow City Cafe
King Crab
Alaskan red king crab from the Bering Sea — legs spanning five feet, meat sweet and dense. Simply steamed or grilled with butter. Anchorage is one of the best places on earth to eat it straight from the source.
Glacier BrewHouse· 10th & M Seafoods
Birch Syrup
A rare Alaskan sweetener requiring 100 gallons of sap per gallon — 25 times the labor of maple. Darker and more complex, with a faint tangy finish. Available in specialty shops downtown and from local producers each spring.
4th Avenue gift shops· 10th & M Seafoods
Food Delivery
DoorDash
Foreign number: not accepted.
Requires a US mobile number at registration — international numbers are rejected. Strong coverage in Anchorage, including late-night delivery from most restaurants on 5th and 6th Avenues. Best selection on the platform; pair with a US SIM if you plan to order frequently.
doordash.com
Uber Eats
Foreign number: accepted.
Works with any international number and card — the easiest option for visitors without a US SIM. Coverage in Anchorage is solid, though slightly smaller than DoorDash's restaurant list. Less useful outside Anchorage, where food delivery options thin out considerably.
ubereats.com
Getting Around
Uber
Foreign number: accepted.
The go-to ride-hailing option in Anchorage — available throughout the city and useful for reaching trailheads outside the walkable centre. Works with international numbers and cards. Coverage drops off sharply outside Anchorage; car rental is the only practical option for Kenai, Seward, or Homer.
uber.com
Lyft
Foreign number: accepted.
Available in Anchorage alongside Uber — driver availability can vary, particularly in the evening, so it's worth having both apps open to compare wait times. Same international-number acceptance as Uber; useful as a backup when surge pricing is high.
lyft.com

Worth Knowing

On Ice and Distance

Anchorage sits at an unusual junction. The 4th Avenue outside the hotel looks like any mid-sized American city — coffee shops, a brewery, a parking structure — but look south and the Chugach Mountains rise in an unbroken wall above the rooftops. The city doesn't gradually give way to wilderness. The edge is immediate and total, and you feel it every time you get into a car heading anywhere interesting.

This guide visits five glaciers. That begins to feel like excess until you learn that Alaska contains roughly 27,000 glaciers covering about 5% of the state's area. The five here — Knik, Matanuska, Portage, Exit, and the Kenai Fjords icepack — represent the most accessible fraction of a system that stores more fresh water than most countries. All five are retreating. The marker stakes at Exit Glacier, planted decade by decade to chart the ice margin, are one of the clearest physical records of climate change anywhere in the world.
